utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could you kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam. The situation has slightly changed from yesterday. I see that Mr. Ostojic is back; Mr. Sarapa is not yet. Otherwise there are no changes. Any preliminaries? I understand there are none. I thank you. It was Mr. Josse who was in possession of the floor. He was just starting his cross-examination. Good morning to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are going to proceed with the cross-examinations today and hopefully finish. We will go our utmost. Thank you so much. Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Does the name Brigadier General van der Wind mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Was he involved in the events at all?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in the events. As far as I recollect, he was in charge of the debriefing back in Holland.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And in that regard, he produced a report; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: As a matter of interest, have you read that report?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you to have a look at an extract from it. It's our Exhibit 6D2. As we can see, it actually says that it's an excerpt from page 45 of what is called "The Report Based on the Debriefing on Srebrenica," dated the 4th of October, 1995. I assume that you'll be able to help us since this report was written in Dutch; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And we can see that paragraph 4.13 talks about: "BiH soldiers, complete with blue caps or blue hats, came within a distance of 15 metres from one of the observation posts. Resembling UN personnel, they opened fire from this position in the direction of the BSA front line, so that it seemed as if the UN had opened fire. In this way, they attempted to draw fire from the BSA on the OP and thus involve DutchBat in the combat actions." Firstly, were you aware of anything like that happening at the time?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It happened a couple of times, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I appreciate it's a long time ago, but are you able to recall when those couple of times --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recollect one occasion where I was personally involved. It was in the surroundings of observation post Alpha and that must have been in February already. And, well, a couple of times it happened but I can't name dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Any recollection of it happening around the fall of the enclave, in July?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And when you became aware of it happening in the earlier part of 1995, what, if anything, did you or Mr. Karremans try to do about it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we protested at the staff of the 28th Division. That's about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: To any avail?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did that have any effect?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no, not that we could discover.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Perhaps I could just ask you: You mentioned this occasion in February, that you personally saw this; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was at OP alpha and then it happened. BiH soldiers about 40, 50 metres away from that observation post started to fire in the direction of BSA positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And to what extent, in your view, did these ABiH soldiers appear as if they were UN troops?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't -- in that case, I couldn't see their outfit. There was -- it was pretty bushy, these surroundings, and there was just firing and we could see there was firing in the direction of the Bosnian Serb positions. And we were very sure we were not doing that, so the only conclusion could be that it would be BiH soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And what about information, either then or subsequently, that BiH soldiers were deliberately putting on blue caps or blue hats to appear as if they were part of your battalion?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recollect one or two reports that we saw a couple of BiH soldiers with a blue berets on distance, by which I mean there were patrols that saw them within 400 or 500 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And have you any idea how they managed to get hold of those blue hats or --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You spent the 10th of July in Potocari; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did you receive any reports from Srebrenica that either ABiH soldiers or alternatively Muslim irregulars were firing from near Bravo Company towards BSA troops?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not specific reports that they did because, on the 10th, we were already trying to start up the defence of the city. And on the 10th, there were still BiH forces in these surroundings and, well, they probably shot at the Serbs when they approached. That's quite clear, yes. And will have been done in the vicinity of my position, my blocking position, as well, but it was not reported to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: But you're saying it's obvious that --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is obvious, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You spoke yesterday about 114 wounded being evacuated from Srebrenica to Potocari on the 11th of July.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Would be I right in saying that you are unable to say how many of those injured had been wounded by reason of the shelling?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know and I don't know whether they all came from Srebrenica. I stated that yesterday as well. When the situation got a bit stable, we counted them and we came to that amount, and where they came from, et cetera. But the mass of these wounded had flesh wounds, and I'm not a doctor so I don't know what the real cause was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did you have any knowledge of some of the wounded having come from the Srebrenica hospital and having --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, some of them came from the hospital because we tried to organise their evacuation. But, again, I don't know numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What I wasn't quite clear about is: The number of 114, that came from one of your doctors, counting them.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My dressing station reported that to me. I didn't count them myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No, of course not.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Josse speak closer into the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I can certainly try.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The 17th of July agreement was signed for what purpose?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In origin, it was on the wish of the Serb forces, of the Serb delegation. And I already stated why I did sign it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Absolutely. As far as you were concerned, to what extent did it relate to the evacuation of the wounded?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, the evacuation of the wounded were in -- the total agreement or a total statement were part of it, and the details of the evacuation of the wounded had to be arranged with ICRC.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Were any UNHCR representatives involved in that meeting?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not as far as I know, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd like to show you another document that describes what I think is this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: But, Your Honour, out of an abundance of caution, perhaps we could go into private session, because it does mention a name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session for a while, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session, Mr. Josse. I thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: As I said a moment ago, Mr. Franken, what I'm now going to ask you about is how you perceived the relationship between your command in north-east sector and also Sarajevo, the relationship between the various personnel and also command centres.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can only tell you what they are both -- their positions was. In Tuzla there was the Sector North-East which, in fact, was commanded by the UN headquarters in Sarajevo. The only thing I can say to that, that one pays in -- the command line, being the Sector North-East, was pretty often forgotten in the end phase, which meant that the next higher command, being Sarajevo, directly ordered DutchBat things, gave them orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Just clarify that in terms of personnel. I think my learned friend Ms. Condon mentioned yesterday Lieutenant Colonel Brantz. He was the DutchBat commander in Tuzla; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, that's incorrect. It is Colonel Brantz. He was Chief of Staff of the command of sector north-east, so that's the next higher echelon in the UN line seen from my battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So he was a full colonel at the time.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a full colonel, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And he was based in Tuzla; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And he was the officer to whom Mr. Karremans was meant to report.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the staff, and he was Chief of Staff of that unit, that we were supposed to report to, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And what was his formal line-of-command relationship with General Nicolai?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was, in fact, the next higher echelon, which meant that General Nicolai was Chief of Staff in Sarajevo, or one of the Chiefs of Staff, but Chief of Staff in Sarajevo, and the next lower level, being headquarters sector north-east, that is where Colonel Brantz was Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And General Nicolai at the time was a brigadier general.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So that's the equivalent to a one-star general in the US Army, for example.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And a colonel is the rank immediately below that, a full colonel, that is.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct again.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did you perceive various problems with communication either with or on the part of sector north-east in the final phase that you have been describing over the last couple of days?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I stated about that before, we had some problems with -- as far as I contacted my higher echelon, it was always the staff of the ops room of the sector north-east, and we had some trouble with them, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And the problem was communication difficulties, in particular, because some of the staff didn't speak sufficiently good English.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the reason was, but to be quite clear, once in a while I had the idea that there were no soldiers at the other side but civilians they just took off the street and didn't know what they were talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm going to quote --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just to put it clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm going to quote what you said to the Dutch parliamentary inquiry into the events in Srebrenica on the 11th of November of 2002. You said: "Certainly, in the final stages, HQ in Sarajevo, i.e., General Nicolai, was acting without the knowledge of sector north-east. The problem with the staff at north-east was that it was an internationally composed staff, a lot of whom had very little English. This led to an awful lot of misunderstandings and the most extraordinary arguments which I shan't bother you with now. I, myself, had a terrible row with a head of operations who claimed that I didn't even have any OPs at all,, because of course, he knew far better than I did." And, in fairness, you went on and said: "Contacts with Lieutenant Colonel Brantz went reasonably smoothly but the usual line contacts through the staff were a disaster. I have no other word for it." Do you stand by that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In other words, what I just stated, so yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did you, in those days in July, personally speak to either Mr. Brantz or Mr. Nicolai?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had one conversation with Colonel Brantz, yes, I remember. But now you're going to ask me when exactly. But somewhere in these days.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: But you didn't personally communicate with Mr. Nicolai --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And I assume you had no communication with sir Rupert Smith either, no personal communication.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I just ask you that for completeness. Did you get the impression that General Nicolai, again towards the end of these events, was giving orders which reflected a slight lack of realism on his part?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At least I had the idea that the orders we got from the UN - and, again, I do not know whether General Nicolai was the person who gave them - but the orders we got Sarajevo led me to the idea that they did not exactly know what was happening or what the situation was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: At a later stage in your evidence at the parliamentary inquiry, I think you said: "During the end phase, the Dutch version of General Nicolai, again first giving the order. And this is quite unusual, to defend the UN unit and its resources, to offer protection or something like it to the population, that you almost got the impression that the man had been out of the picture for a few days, as we say." Again --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the same, what I said, only in these days I was a bit more diplomatic, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And which order specifically are you referring to? Can you remember?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I remember that it was specifically about the order that we had to defend the city and then we were ordered to, what is called, assist in the evacuation. And then in the morning we got an order to defend again, and two hours later we got the guidelines of how to assist in the evacuation, just one example.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I thank you so much, Mr. Josse. I think it's Madam Fauveau who is next. Madam Fauveau is defending General Miletic. Madam Fauveau, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Franken, you mentioned the supply of DutchBat or supplies, and you said that your request for supplies was sent to Sarajevo. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: My request went directly to my logistics base in Busovaca and they proceeded that to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can it be said that you did not send your request for supplies directly to the organs of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And when a request was granted, that supplies would arrive, did you receive notification of this authorisation through your command, through the United Nations command? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I got the confirmation of a convoy directly from my logistics base I mentioned before.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: But, at any rate, you would not receive it directly from the organs of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you know who within Republika Srpska was in charge of granting authorisations for convoys?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You also stated that the convoys would start from Tuzla or Sarajevo. Is it correct to say that they would leave from territories controlled by the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it also correct to say that they had to go through a check-point of the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a check-point, but on the Bosnian -- on the BiH side they were not controlled or inspected.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it correct to say that, at some point, the DutchBat would get supplies from Bratunac, from Fontana Hotel?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I'm aware of. No, it's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: So DutchBat never bought any goods from the Fontana Hotel for the members of the DutchBat?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not as far as I recollect.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Well, you stated that you had major problems in terms of fuel. Is it right to say that, at the time, the UNHCR had stocks of fuel that were stocked there in the Potocari compound?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. UNHCR had fuel and MSF had some fuel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can we be more specific as regards the time-frame, please, Mr. Franken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Was the situation always the same at any given moment, or did it change as we went along or at any other time that you may be able to specify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. In March, Your Honour, UNHCR and MSF had stocks of fuel on the compound.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it right to say that you used the fuel stocks belonging to the UNHCR?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it also right to say that the UNHCR and MSF still had fuel in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct, because we totally used their supplies during March, April.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You stated that one of the DutchBat tasks was to facilitate distribution of humanitarian aid in the enclave, and you said that the UNHCR convoys had problems when it came to entering the enclave. But is it not fair to say that, at some point in time, the UNHCR convoys had problems with the DutchBat?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's absolutely not right, because there were no problems between UNHCR and DutchBat.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness be shown Exhibit 5D54. Can we turn to page 4, last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can you read the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. You mean aloud?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, no. We don't need any reading lessons. Just read it for yourself and then Madam Fauveau will be asking you a question.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. That's what I had in mind.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it this a fair description of the events?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It has to do with the situation that the BiH wanted to arrange check-points themselves, and I forbid that and gave them the guarantee that we would check all NGO vehicles coming in the enclave. And probably this is the consequence of that. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that the UNHCR representatives were not very happy with the situation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That is fair, but we talked about that and they understood. So I do not see that as a problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: But is it right to say, however, that some UNHCR convoys that were destined to the enclave did not arrive in the enclave precisely because of the searches carried out by the DutchBat?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness be shown page 5 of the same document.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Please have a quick look at the paragraph starting with the words "On 20th June ..."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you remember this convoy that was turned back to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not because I didn't turn back. Probably UNHCR itself did.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: At any rate, you would allow for the possibility that the UNHCR returned this convoy to Belgrade because of search or searches carried out by DutchBat.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I read here, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: With regard to the supplies to the enclave, can it be said that the Serbs offered to come to an agreement with the Muslim authorities to supply the enclave?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. There was a proposition of the Serbs to start up some trade.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And such proposition would involve all kinds of goods but for weapons; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can it be said that this was never really materialised because of the objections or opposition by the military leaders in the enclave?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it also right to say that there was a black market throughout your stay in the enclave?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were goods sold at the marketplace, yes, cigarettes and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And can it also be said that a large part of the humanitarian aid coming into the enclave was taken by the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stated that before. When a supply came in, there was a part reserved for the 28th Division, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: But is it possible that the Serbs knew that part of the humanitarian aid would be directed to the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything is possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You also mentioned MSF, Medecins Sans Frontieres. You said that this organisation was responsible for medical care provided in the enclave. Isn't it fair to say that at some point in time there was a conflict between the town authorities and MSF?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And this conflict arose in March 1995, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Somewhere in that period, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it also right to say that at that time, because of the conflict, MSF stopped looking after the population, providing medical care?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it right to say that they even refused allowing local doctors to use their medical supplies?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recollect details like that, but I know they stopped their aid.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And is it right to say that, during this conflict, DutchBat doctors also had some problems in terms of providing medical care to the local population?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, yes and no. I'll explain that. My surgeons had problems to go to the civilian hospital, because they tried to join the MSF, in their point of view, but the medical care we directly gave to the population was not stopped for that reason. We had to stop that a couple of weeks earlier because of the lack of fuel. We had our mobile, what do you call it, Red Cross point, aid points, in several villages which were visited each week, but we had to stop that aid. What stopped as a consequence of the conflict were my surgeons who, in fact, refused to go to the hospital because they took the side of the MSF.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it right to say that, during that period, starting in March or April 1995 until the fall of the enclave, there were enough medicines in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer will be in two parts. One, the medical supplies of the battalion were on the lowest level acceptable. That's why we stopped supporting the civilians as well. I'm not exactly aware of the supplies MSF had, but the hospital stayed open. I do not exactly know with what supplies, or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Are you aware of a problem in terms of medical supplies in January and in February 1995?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean supplies of the battalion or you mean supplies for Medecins Sans Frontieres?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I mean medical supplies for the battalion.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In January, when I arrived, they were at an acceptable -- the necessary level.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown Exhibit 5D53. Can we turn to page 4.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Please have a look at the paragraph starting with, "On 10 April ..." and then the one after that.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Does this paragraph remind you of the events in January 1995?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which event do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Well, the lack of medical supplies.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, in January, we were at an acceptable level, acceptable is that we could support our own battalion, and that altered, obviously, in April. In January, March -- no, wrong. In February, March, we had to stop the support to the local population. And then, as it's stated here, in April we resumed that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: However, in this document, the opposite is said. In this paragraph, starting with, "On 10 April," it looks as though after April 1995 there were enough supplies, even too many.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: After April 1995. It looks in this paragraph like that, but I can absolutely assure you that we had a level up of the supplies. And in the end we had the iron -- only the iron stock and below that. And the iron stock, I stated above that before, it was the minimum level acceptable to guarantee medical support to the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it right to say that, indeed, 90 per cent of medical supplies were used to provide medical care to the local population?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know. I absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And do you know that some members of the ABiH were treated in the medical premises of DutchBat?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You mentioned OP Echo taken by the Serbs on the 8th of June, 1995. Is it not fair to say that OP Echo was in a location used by the Muslims to get out of the enclave?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct. As far as we know, the area directly -- or 1 or 2 kilometres west of OP Echo was used. We didn't have -- in the beginning we didn't have any observation post there.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Isn't it fair to say that the Muslims used the people positioned on OP Echo in order to be protected when they would leave the enclave?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that is correct. What we know is that they used the location of OP Echo to get wood and things out of the local furniture factory, which was in front of OP Echo.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When you said they used the factory, who do you have in mind, the Serbs or the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had the Muslims in mind, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And this factory used by the Muslims, was it in the territory controlled by the Serb army?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The problem with this factory was that the UN border went right through it. There was a part in the Serb armed area and there was a part in the Muslim area. Above that, there were two other borders. There was a Serb border, which obviously was in that location so that the complete factory was within Serb territory, and there was a Muslim border going further south with the opposite result.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did the Serbs try to intervene in order to solve the problem arising around the factory?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they protested with us that what the Muslims were looting, that, what they said, Serb factory, and on that occasion, I had contact with Major Nikolic. I said, "Okay, we can stop that but just let me have the gear to stop it." I asked him to allow a convoy coming in with -- well, means, like barbed wire, et cetera, to close that factory down at our side, at the north side, so the Muslims wouldn't be able to come in anymore. But I never got that material because a request for resupply with these things was denied.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that the headquarters of the 28th Division was in the very city of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had, more or less, two headquarters. There was one classroom they used in the village of Potocari and they used some rooms in the former post office of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it, therefore, fair to say that they used civilian buildings for military purposes?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as did DutchBat.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that Lieutenant Colonel Karremans informed you of the fact that, in the evening of the 10th of July, he had seen about 1.500 armed men in the centre of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You stated that Srebrenica had been bombed on the 10th of July, or shelled. Would you allow for the possibility that these armed men would have been the target of the Serb army?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And is it also possible that the headquarters of the 28th Division would have been the target of this shelling?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is possible, but I have to make one remark: Then they were very poor gunners because they hit the whole city instead of those two locations.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You mentioned some brigades of the 28th Division. Do you know where their HQ was?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was not recognisable as such.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You mentioned an ultimatum delivered by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was Exhibit P2264. Can it be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: It is, indeed, the transcription of a radio message that you received or that you interpreted as being a Serb ultimatum.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: What language did you receive this message in?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: By radio, in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And the individual who delivered the message did not introduce themselves, did they?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only, myself, heard a part of -- the last part of that radio message, and I don't know whether he identified himself or what.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In reality, you had no possibility, no means, to say exactly that the person delivering the message was a member of the republic -- of the VRS, of BSA.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Therefore, you do not know at all what the origin of this message is.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the only thing I knew was that it came through our means on our frequency, and so it is, to use your words, fair to say that it's probably sent out of our APCs taken by the Bosnian Serbs, armoured personnel carriers.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Let us assume that it came from your vehicle, but you don't know whether your vehicle had been taken by regular forces or by irregular forces.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. We had no possibilities to verify whether this was, by the BSA, an authorised message, if that is what you're looking for.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that the Srebrenica population wanted to be evacuated out of Srebrenica to Potocari?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And is it also right to say that the DutchBat decided, made a decision, to evacuate the population from Srebrenica to Potocari?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We led the way to our camp. That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When you decided to evacuate the population to Potocari, did you have any idea of what was to happen, to ensue?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We were not -- we couldn't be sure about what was going to happen.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: But you knew, at any rate, that these people could not stay in Potocari, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they could stay for a short period, but that was not an issue at that very moment. I had to take, pretty swiftly, measures to stop the situation in the city of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Granted. But, anyway, the shifting of the population to Potocari was a temporary measure, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that Lieutenant Colonel Karremans turned to the BSA in order to obtain aid in order to evacuate the population from Potocari to territories held by the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing I know is that he went there and asked for help, in fact, and the rest I'm not aware of. I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it right to say that DutchBat members were supposed to help in the evacuation and that they had to check that -- one of their main tasks was to check who, among the population, wanted to remain in the former enclave?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's incorrect. We were supposed to help or to facilitate the evacuation. We spoke to the population through that committee, and they -- it was not our task to ask every individual whether he wanted to go or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I'm not suggesting that it was your task to ask each and every individual, but at any rate, your task was to see whether there was a part of the population, some people, who wanted to stay. Can it be expressed in this way?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Again, it was not my task to check that. We had representatives, they represented the population, and the wishes of that population came through these representatives. My order to help was to assist in the practical execution of the evacuation.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown Exhibit 1D33. This is the prior statement by the witness to the OTP on the 26th and 27th of September, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can we turn to page 4, last sentence. Please, sir, could you read this sentence, saying, [In English] "We had to check who wanted to stay in the enclave." [Interpretation] It's the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it. But let me have the context, please. Just hold. I want to read the paragraph above as well. Thank you. As I read this sentence, that it is a wish of Mladic or the Bosnian Serbs that we had to check and it was not in my orders from the UN.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Since you had a look at the context, can you confirm that, indeed, you uttered this sentence after the first meeting Lieutenant Colonel Karremans had with General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just hold, please. I can't find what you're referring to. Just hold. If you mean that I did utter the sentence, "we had to check who wanted to stay in the enclave," then that is correct; that, as stated here, it would have been after the first meeting. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sorry, maybe there was a mistake. My mistake. It was after the second meeting, but at any rate it was in the evening of the 11th of July.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is as I read it here, yes, because I do not remember details like that now.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did you personally see or did any Dutch member report that there were people in Potocari who wanted to remain in the former enclave?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not, nor, to my knowledge, did any Dutch member of DutchBat.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you know or were you made aware of the fact that some people did not want to go to Kladanj, that they wanted to go somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was not made aware of that and I did not know, because there originally was given a possibility. As I recollect, Mladic said that they could point out the direction they want to go themselves, but in later agreement or negotiations or briefings, it was said that they would go to Kladanj. And discussions about the direction or destination I did not take part of, I do not know of.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When you say later on, when Kladanj was mentioned, did that happen after the meeting to which some representative of the Muslim population, including Mr. Mandzic, were present together with Mladic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether Kladanj was mentioned in the second meeting or the third meeting in the morning of the 12th. I don't recollect that anymore, but ...

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And you personally, you did not attend the meeting, did you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was -- no, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And you don't know whether it is likely that the Muslim representative had requested to go to Kladanj.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can it be said that, on the 12th of July, when the buses arrived, the people, the population, really were in a hurry to get on board the buses?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can it also be said that, to your knowledge, nobody was forced to get into buses?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in that stage, at the beginning. There was, later on, some force used by Bosnian Serb soldiers to get a hell of a lot of people in a bus, which we reacted on by preparing busloads, so to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Indeed, what you say is that some soldiers wanted that to be done more quickly, but nobody was against boarding the buses, were they?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In general, I didn't experience that they were against bussing, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it right to say that you personally did not witness the separation of men of able-bodied men from their families?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. I only saw the result.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You even received reports, for instance, in the evening of the 12th or in the morning of the 13th of July, saying that the men, including men, did arrive in Kladanj?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was in the late afternoon of the 12th. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown 5 D76?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, this is a report dated 12th July 1995 and you had an opportunity to see it during your interview with the OTP in 2003. You then said that this report seemed to be genuine and that it was exact. Could you read it again and confirm that it is a report that is exact?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That describes exactly the situation at that moment. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And during your testimony, you mentioned Mr. Nuhanovic, who was a member of the Muslim delegation. He was the father of one of the UNMO interpreters. Is it fair to say that you saw Mr. Nuhanovic senior go with his family, boarding a bus?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. I was -- I accompanied him until about 30 metres out of our main gate.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Were you able to see that he got on the bus together with his family?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness be shown -- oh, before I ask for this document I have another set of questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You mentioned the bodies of nine men you were informed about by Coster. Could you tell me whether, after being informed about the bodies, whether the bodies were buried?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They were out of our UN area and we did not bury the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Isn't it fair to say that at least one person committed suicide during these two days? And the person who committed suicide, was the person buried?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry. Yes, both are correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Why did the person who committed suicide get buried whilst the other nine bodies were just left there?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the man was in one of the factory halls within our UN territory and the nine bodies were about, yeah, well, about 100, 150 metres out and we couldn't go there freely, because the discovery of these bodies was done by a sneaky patrol. And we were not able to go out there, what do you call it, to bury the bodies in any place or to pick them up.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Lastly, I would like to show you Exhibit P453. This is the statement you signed on the 17th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we turn to the last page, just before the signatures. I think this is the last part of page 1, which is the English version. I'm sorry. There is also a signed version. I'm sorry. We can -- then it would be page 3. Can we see page 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, is it fair to say that you had some comments on this agreement which you added at the end of this statement?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And the Serbs did agree to you mentioning your comments in the body of the statement.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I stated before, the lawyer in the Serb delegation got a bit, what do you call that, mad about that, and there was a short and pretty tough discussion within the Serb delegation after my writing that sentence to the ...

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, is it fair to say that this declaration was not signed by members of the BSA?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my knowledge, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: It was, indeed, on the Serb side, signed by Mr. Deronjic, who was the representative of the civilian authorities in Srebrenica, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was presented to me as being the new civil authority of Srebrenica, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, you made a statement to the OTP on the 17th of October, 2003. You then said that the Sector North-East report -- I mean, I can show you this but I don't think it's necessary. You said that those reports were, to a large part, sort of, based on the reports they would get from you. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the report that Sector North-East sent to his higher echelons about the situation in Srebrenica? That was absolutely based on our information, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did you send reports on a daily basis to the Sector North-East?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, several. There was quite an extended reporting system within the UN channels.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And would you also receive information from the Sector North-East as to what had happened on other fronts in BiH?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we generally got those. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: But for the reports you would send to the Sector North-East, did you also send reports to the Dutch authorities?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was not a reporting line to the Dutch authorities. Periodically, there was contact to The Hague when it was thought to be necessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And such contacts would be done orally, or was there some sort of written trace of it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean the contacts to The Hague, as far as I know, they were orally.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When you left the enclave, what happened to the documents you had within DutchBat?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as stated before, we had the order from the UN to destroy documents and archives and even our computers. We did not complete that task completely, so what was left was brought along to Zagreb and later on to Holland.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did you know why the order had been given to destroy the documents, the archives?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I estimated it as being a form of panic or something.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And do you remember who gave you the order? Did it come from Sarajevo, from Tuzla or from Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, sir. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Fauveau. There are two Defence teams left, Mr. Haynes and Mr. Meek. I don't know who is going first. Have you -- I think if you -- we will have a break in about seven, eight minutes' time, Mr. Haynes. And you -- he broke the lectern now. I think we need a break. I think we need a break. It's all right. Thank you. Mr. Haynes is appearing for General Pandurevic and he will be cross-examining you. Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Franken. I'm going to ask you a few quick questions up to the break, and then there will come a natural point because I will need my case manager to go into the front row to show you a video. I want to ask you a few questions, to start off with, about fuel. You told us on Monday that by July of 1995, the battalion was surviving on 250 litres of fuel per day.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: We've heard from Mr. Boering that none of the OPs around the enclave ever became inoperative in the sense that you weren't able to provide power to them.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct as well. The OPs had their own stocks and they went down to a minimum level as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: And they should think about a daily use of 8 to 10 litres.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: That's very helpful. Because each of the OPs had its own generator, didn't it --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: -- to provide it power? And would that have been a similar generator to that which provided power to your headquarters in Srebrenica itself, or would that have been a larger generator?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Srebrenica we had very large generators.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And the general level of consumption of that generator would have been what?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. I only can -- I knew the figure. We figured out the total use of the battalion a day, what was necessary, and I really don't know the details, how many litres that specific generator used during a couple of hours, or something.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, you probably pre-empted my next question which might have been a little unfair, which was, I am going to ask you what the total reservoir of your vehicles was in terms of diesel fuel.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Because you also said that the daily requirement of the battalion was 8.000 to 9.000 litres of fuel.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Or, putting it another way, 9 tonnes.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: A bit less, because --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes. And was that the sort of level of order of fuel you were making to your superior command to be delivered to you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We ordered amounts, based on experience, of what, when it came through, was allowed by the Serbs, and we tried to make stocks -- to perform stocks on the base for even the worst times.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And it's right to say - you've answered this question fairly, I think, to a number of other people - that for the first three or four months of your tour of duty, there were no difficulties with supplies at all, were there?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: February, as I remember, we had a last fuel convoy coming in. That's why I started afterwards using the UNHCR stocks. And, in general, the first couple of months we got regularly resupplied, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And the sort of levels of resupply were in many, many tonnes per week.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not constant on the week. That was the strange thing. All at once we got a couple of convoys and then there was a silence of a couple of weeks that we couldn't get anything, et cetera. So it was not -- you couldn't count on when a convoy came in and with what.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you told Madam Fauveau a little while ago something about the black market trade that was taking place between those within the enclave and those outside the enclave.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry. As I referred to the black market question, I meant goods that were sold in the marketplace in Srebrenica, sold by Muslim people to Muslim people, and I had a question about the offer of the Serbs to start up trade with the Muslims within the enclave. So there are two things.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, I'm asking you about trade between those within the enclave and those outside the enclave.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: That began during your tour of duty, didn't it? Or there was a discussion about that --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a discussion. The Serbs proposed that and then we tried to arrange meetings at OP Papa between the Serbs and the Muslims, and they had to come to an agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And were you conscious that trade did take place between Muslims within the enclave and Serbs outside?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not through these arrangements anyway, because that was stopped by the Bosnian Muslim authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Right. I'm going to ask you whether you were ever aware that fuel was being sold by Muslims within the enclave to Serbs outside the enclave?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, in that event, that ends that particular line of questioning, and that may be a sensible moment to take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, Mr. Haynes and Mr. Franken. We will reconvene in 25 minutes' time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Why is the witness not here? Why is the witness not here?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understood that one of the counsel for the accused had an issue they wanted to raise pertaining to a document that I had advised them I wished to use on redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then why don't we leave that until the witness has finished his testimony? You raise it in his absence, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, it's a document that the Prosecution intends to use in its redirect with that witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Why interrupt the cross-examination? I mean it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: We just believed it was the proper time, to do it now, rather than while he's sitting there, to have those arguments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's hear the submissions now. Who wishes to make submissions? Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. First of all, Mr. President, I'd like to say I'm grateful to my colleague for providing in advance this document that he intends to use during his redirect. This is a new document that is not on the Rule 65 ter list. Now, of course, there are competing theories here, whether the Prosecution can use new documents as part of its redirect. We believe that the Prosecution cannot use a document that is not on its Rule 65 ter list, even though it is in redirect, of course, unless we would have used the document during cross-examination, which we haven't done. This is a document, it is in agreement, that the witness referred to yesterday between General Mladic and General Smith. General Smith being a witness in this case, we find that we have problems understanding why this document was not put on the Rule 65 ter list of the Prosecution in the first place, give that General Smith is a witness. Now, this is their choice. When they do that Rule 65 ter list, they elect to take some documents and not to take some documents. Now, this document in this case was disclosed to the Defence at some point in the past during the pre-trial phase, but it was not put on the Rule 65 ter list, and at this point we say that this should not be allowed. Now, with this specific document, the Defence, we spoke amongst each other, and we do not intend to object to this specific document being used in the present circumstances. However, what is important to us is that we want to make sure that we adopt a position and principle about what documents can and cannot be used by the Prosecution as part of redirect when it's a document that has not been used in cross-examination by the Defence and when it's a document that was not on its Rule 65 ter list. That's the issue that we wanted to bring to the attention of the Trial Chamber. But we understand, given the nature of this document, at one point or another, it will come in as evidence. It is highly relevant and it falls in the category of those documents maybe that, yes, everybody, all parties, have an interest in having on board. But that is not to say that for future documents the same position will be adopted by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, Mr. Bourgon. Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. I have no explanation for why the document is not on the 65 ter list. However, this, as my learned colleague has already indicated, was disclosed six months ago to the Defence. It is relevant evidence that goes to an issue that I did not lead this witness on. I believe that the door was opened. It's just a short few questions about the document. That is why I supplied it, in advance of his testimony, to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, two points: First of all, I would like to see how my learned friend deals with it in re-examination to make sure that it's strictly relevant and it arises from questions asked by the Defence; and secondly, it is an important document; it's clearly going to be admitted into evidence. What I'd invite the Chamber to do is, if the questions from the Prosecution invite further questions from the Defence, for to us have the right to further cross-examine upon the document and solely upon the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's have a very short recess, two minutes or so, to discuss this last point. As regards the guideline that should govern your conduct in the future in such like occasions, we don't need to come down with that today, but we agree with you, Mr. Bourgon, that guidelines are called for. And, mind you, it's a matter of law that we can only repeat to you, because it's not something new that has fallen down on us from heaven today. But we would prefer to formalise it once it has been raised. As regards whether there should be an opportunity for further cross-examination following the re-examination by your learned colleague, I think I need to consult my colleagues. We'll be back with you in a minute or so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will be back to you in a minute. --- Break taken at 11.09 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. To answer your question, Mr. Josse, our decision is: If it will be the case, we will allow further cross-examination, only limited to the questions and answers that would have followed in relation to this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, Mr. Haynes -- let's get the witness first, yes. As regards the question you raised, Mr. Bourgon, I mean our position, more or less, is that, as I explained to you before, this is a matter that is generally dealt with under our rules. You know what the position is. Our position is that we will deal with each case as it arises depending on the particulars of each case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. Franken, for having been patient with us. Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Mr. Franken, so that you're clear, I think I have four short topics to deal with you and then I'll be done, okay? The first of those is about a specific requirement of your mission. Did you, during the course of your tour of duty, receive regular details from the Muslim forces within the enclave as to where they had placed land mines?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we did not get information like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So that we are clear, I used the word "regular." Did you receive any reports as to where they had placed land mines?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, none at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Were you aware, for example, through your liaison officers, that land mines were being placed by the Muslim forces around and outside the enclave?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We got information from DutchBat II that there were locations where land mines were.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And did you ask the Muslim forces if they would tell you where they had placed them?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That has been asked but we didn't get an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I take it that land mines were no part of your battalion's arsenal?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And you had no idea where the forces within the enclave were obtaining land mines to place elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's very helpful. The next point I want to move on to is your knowledge of Srebrenica itself. You're plainly somebody who, between January and July 1995, visited many parts, many buildings, within the town.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many parts of the town, yes. Buildings is -- I only was in the town hall.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Srebrenica wasn't an exclusively Muslim town during the time of your tour of duty, was it? There were some Serbs who lived there.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We heard that there were still some Serbs, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And there was, for example, within the town of Srebrenica an Orthodox church and an Orthodox cemetery?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a church, yes. The cemetery was a bit north of Srebrenica town.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you visit, yourself, the church and/or the cemetery?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not visit the church. I saw that cemetery every time I went to Srebrenica because it was alongside the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Right. And what state was it in?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not destroyed, if you mean that. Well, poor maintenance, but not destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Okay. I'll move on from there. Can we move on to the question of arms? When you arrived with DutchBat III at Srebrenica, would you have said your battalion was fully and adequately armed?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What sort of small-arms provision did you have per man? How many rounds per man did you have?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We should have had 450, and when we started we had up and about 120.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: That's the number of rounds per man. And at that time you had, I think, in excess of 400 soldiers.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So we can calculate -- I can't, but somebody can calculate exactly how many rounds of small-arms fire you had.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Would you expect that sort of munition to degrade during the course of the time that you were there?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It degrades pretty quickly when you use it under, what we call, operational circumstances, which means it is in magazines and in the weapon and carried around.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And were there no storage facilities for your small arms munitions?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had storage facilities, being a sea container.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And were they used?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As far as we had anything in it, it was used, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can we move on to, as it were, the lodgeable weaponry you had. You had anti-tank weapons, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And they were still operative in July of 1995.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of them, they were not, which -- I had three kinds, in fact. We had TOW, referred to before.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had the Dragan. And we had the 84; it's a portable man-held weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: The essential difficulty with anti-tank weapons in July of 1995 was the terrain, wasn't it? They were unsuited to the hilly terrain, particularly to the south of the enclave.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not the problem. The major problem was the state they were in technically, the weapons system, and the proper ammunition for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Right. I mean, speaking generically, if these things become degraded, they are inaccurate and rather dangerous to fire.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the TOW is concerned, you can't fire it; as far as the Dragon is concerned, as soon as the ammo is not in good quality any more, you can't fire it as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Right. I'm going to move on to the last topic now. Just to preface it, on the 10th of July, you were in Srebrenica itself, in the town.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 10th, I was in Potocari headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Right. And the 11th as well.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. And so everything that you learned or everything that you've told us about, the battle situation on the 10th and the 11th of July, is what you've gleaned from reports from your subordinates.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and direct radio contact with the company commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Right. I'm going to summarise, as it were, the position at a number of the OPs on the 11th of July. I don't want to take you to the document, but I've taken this from your debriefing document --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: -- so I hope you'll agree with it. OP Echo found itself in a position where the Bosnian Serb forces had taken the adjacent high land.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: And OP Echo was withdrawn, was not in place any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: OP Foxtrot, the Bosnian Serb army had taken all the surrounding area and there was a tank within 60 yards of the OP itself.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At the 10th, OP Foxtrot was abandoned, withdrawn as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: OP Sierra was surrounded.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Sierra, in the course of the 10th, was surrounded. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And OP Kilo found the Bosnian Serb forces behind them.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: OP November was surrounded and OP Papa was on the Serb territory anyway?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: More or less on Serb territory, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: You'd agree with that summary.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, the OP offers some form of protection against adjacent fire, doesn't it? It's, to an extent, dug in and it's protected by sandbagging.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, well, they had a kind of sandbagging. Defence walls, it was called, were big, more or less, containers with sand and stone in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: But it's not such a structure that it would survive a direct hit from a rocket or a shell or mortar fire.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They proved to be not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No. In relation to all of the OPs that I've mentioned, let's not put too fine a point on it, if the Bosnian Serb forces had wanted to blow those OPs off the face of earth, they could have done.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They could and, in a couple of cases, did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we move on to the question of APCs? Your APCs were equally vulnerable, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were not. They were vulnerable for tank fire but less vulnerable for artillery and mortar fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: All right. You've referred to one which was, as it were, hijacked. The only other one you lost was the one that went off the road.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I lost all the APCs off the OPs, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Of course. They were abandoned.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were taken along to Bratunac, the major part of it. So I lost about 15 or 16, and, as I recollect, three by fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: The APC that you referred to that had been driven off the road, I think we have some video of and I'd like you to see it now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It's the Srebrenica trial video. It's at 2054.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you.
