utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I don't think it gets any more illuminating than that. A few simple points. You'd agree with me that there is no evidence that that vehicle has been hit by --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't see holes on this side of the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And neither did you see, as it were, holes on the road or trees falling across it or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On this picture I did not see that; that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I dare say, down the course of the years, Mr. Franken, soldiers, young soldiers, have told you a number of things to excuse their incompetence.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but -- you mean in that stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, I mean that looks like an APC that's just been driven off the road, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It looks like an APC that's next to the road, and I can't in this picture see what the cause was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No, okay. Can we move on to the question of your men? You described to us yesterday briefly the injuries suffered by the men under your command. I think you said there were some who had shrapnel injuries.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Do we take it that you had no men who had been injured by small-arms fire?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not as I recollect.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And can we also take it that the shrapnel injuries you referred to are relatively minor injuries?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I stated, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They stayed in position.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I have no further questions for you. Thank you, Mr. Franken.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Haynes. It's Mr. Meek or Mr. Ostojic? Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: With the Court's permission I'd like to ask, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, who is representing the accused Beara, will now be cross-examining you. How long do you expect to be cross-examining the witness, Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: About 40 minutes -- 30 minutes, 40 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I take it, Mr. McCloskey, that you have the next witness here in line.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, we do, Mr. President. Ms. Soljan has that witness and he is outside, ready to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's perfect. Yes, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Franken.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, let me first apologise to you for not being here for your entire testimony. I did have an opportunity, however, to review it, and I'd like to ask you some questions. I hope not to be repetitive, and I'm sure you and the Court will remind me if I am.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'd like to focus quickly just on a general theme and that is reporting from subordinates that you received. I know earlier today, on page 30, specifically lines 18 and 19, for my learned colleague, you said that "there was quite an extended reporting system within the UN channels." When you say "extended," it's really "extensive"; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I just want to make sure. Now, how about the subordinates, the soldiers within DutchBat III that were immediately under you as the second in charge at that time, what were the reporting requirements for them?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on company level, we had, in fact, the UN system, a derivative of the system we used to our higher echelons. There was a standard patrol report they had to fill in when they came back from a patrol. It was filled in in a debrief. And they had -- I don't exactly know the interval any more, but the OPs had to report every X hours the situation. That was crossed by incidents, of course. And that, again, was a UN system, close firing, detonations, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you have or put in place any other system, other than that system by the UN?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We used our normal military way of communication, which means they are on a radio net, and as soon as something happens, they come on the net and report it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, I understood that. My question was: Did you require any different reporting mechanism or reporting data other than that which was required by the UN?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, with respect to why the reporting was necessary, can you explain that to me a little bit.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably everybody had a need of information, and that system tried to supply that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. And it was significant information; is that we are talking about? That's really what your subordinates were reporting to you, items that were significant; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And they would report to you if they saw an increase in arms by either one side or the other side; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, whatever, or firing from a position, et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And the purpose of that, of reporting significant information, is so that you, as the second in charge, as well as your commander, Mr. Karremans - I think I'm pronouncing his name somewhat correctly --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: -- is that you could distil that information and make decisions based on that significant information; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was only -- the first analysing of this information was done by the operations room, and if there was something special, they would report to me. I didn't get every detailed information because that was almost impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you share with us some examples of significant matters that should have been reported by your subordinates to you? Just highlight a few, if you don't mind.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. Yes. Close firing was important, which meant that UN locations or patrols were fired at; observations of armed men within the area; shelling of locations or villages; things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Would it also -- thank you. Would it also be a significant point to report by your subordinate if they were taken hostage by either one or the other side?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That would be very important, in fact; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Would it be significant to report by your subordinate to you whether or not they found a land mine?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I tried to give a summary of all unusual events. Everything which was not usual, they had to report.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And that would be highly unusual and very significant and very important.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. For instance, mines, I got quite a lot of reports about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, or now Colonel, Boering, he was a subordinate at the time under you; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And did he report to you as well, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Summaries of debriefings of talks he had with either side.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, that's also significant, meetings that he may have held with either VRS military personnel or ABiH military personnel; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or ABiH, the civil opstina, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm not limiting it outside of military, but thank you for that. And were those reports given to you verbally or in writing?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Usually verbally. He made notes and that was archived, but I always heard verbal reports. It's quicker and you can ask questions immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. I read in the some of the reports that you believed that Colonel Boering was mistaken about an incident involving the "White House" on or about July 13th as to who ordered UNMO to continue to observe what was occurring at that "White House". Do you remember that at all?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, do you know who ordered the UNMOs to keep an eye on the situation at the "White House" on or about July 13th?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Do you have that independent recollection, as you sit here today; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, do you remember a report from any of your subordinates, including Mr. Boering -- Colonel Boering, excuse me, whether or not he was ever involved in an ambush?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The only thing that could refer to that is the story I heard later on, when he went with the first convoy through the CL, in the area of Kladanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And that was approximately in July of 1995; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he went along with the first convoy. It was even on the 12th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We know exactly --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: But, I mean, I only heard that when I was back in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I understand. Aside from that, the reason you may not have received the report of that ambush is because Colonel Boering was escorting that convoy and that he remained and went to Zagreb thereafter, so you --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: -- didn't have immediate contact with him. That's reasonable; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So he didn't report that to you because he didn't come back until --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I heard that afterwards when I was already out of the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How about March and April of 1995? Do you have a recollection, sir, of any subordinate telling you that they were ambushed by either VRS or ABiH soldiers or civilians?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not. But I must say that, in March, I was on leave during -- ten days in Holland, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How about any time from March to April --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you: Did you ever receive a report upon your return from your leave or while you there, end of March, April, 1995 period, of any of your subordinates having been forced to walk across a minefield?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And that's something that is so significant --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I should remember when it was reported to me, but no.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's fair, and I think I agree with you. Do you recall reporting by any of your subordinates, including Mr. Boering, that he was forced to walk on a plank of wood over a land mine in early March, late April 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please pause between answer and question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please allow a brief pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. I thought I paused but obviously not enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But the interpreters require a greater pause or a longer pause. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: To answer that question, no, I do not know of a story like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How about -- despite the fact that you may have been on holiday for ten or so days in March of 1995, would you have been apprised of that if it occurred upon your return from holiday?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I should say I would be very surprised when they did not, if they did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How about any of your subordinates being kidnapped? Would you -- did you know whether or not any of them were ever kidnapped or held hostage in March and April of 1995?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar, sir, with the check-point called check-point Jovo?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yellow Bridge, yes, I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yellow Bridge; correct. It was called check-point Jovo because one of the men who actually manned that check-point was named Jovo; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I wanted to make sure.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no, no, no. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know, have you ever visited check-point Jovo, or the Yellow Bridge?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. We are going to slow down a little bit.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We will get through this, I think, rather quickly. How often would you say, sir, during your tenure at Srebrenica, did you visit check-point Jovo?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The inside, as I recollect, only once.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. How often would you pass check-point Jovo during your tenure in Srebrenica, from January through July 1995?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was coming in, my leave, so to and going out, so it's about four times.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir, if there were any land mines on or around check-point Jovo?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I had a conference -- because I have to correct myself. I was twice in Jovo, or in that check-point, I should say. The last time I came there, they were land mines on the road, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And when was that, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm just trying to recollect, sorry. Must be anywhere in -- I wasn't there. Must be somewhere in April, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'd like to direct your attention, sir, to the evacuation in July of 1995, if I may.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You testified earlier today, on page 25, lines 12 through 13, for my learned friends, "My order to help was to assist in the practical evacuation --" I'm sorry, I'll start it over. "My order to help was to assist in the practical execution of the evacuation." Do you recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: When you say "assist," is it fair to say that you mean to cooperate?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, to cooperate with the aim that it would have been done in the most humanitarian and legalised way, et cetera. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you also mean to support the evacuation when you use the words "to assist"?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, supported and then in the extent that we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, the Serbs, during the period of evacuation, were they given permission to evacuate the people out of Potocari?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether I understand your question, but as far as I know, Mladic came to the people and said that they were to be evacuated. That's pretty shortly before the first convoy rolled out. And so they were given permission, yes. They were facilitating it, so that is what I understand as giving permission, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I may, with the Court's permission and the assistance of the usher, place Exhibit 2D18 on the ELMO or on the e-court, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: While they are doing that, sir, if I may proceed with a couple of questions. This is my understanding of a chapter in a book entitled, "In the Name of Peace" that you authored, and it's called "A Retrospective View." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember me writing a part of that book, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: When did you write it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably in 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You're right. I understand. Within a year or so of the events; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Why did you write it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On request of the composer of the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'd like to direct your attention to page 3 of this document, and it's the first full paragraph, if I may. I understand and read that this issue was covered by my learned colleagues, but I have a couple of questions, if I may, to ask you about that.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So I'll give you an opportunity to read it and let me know when you've had that opportunity and I'll proceed.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'm directing your attention to the last three or so sentences of that full paragraph, starting with the words, "And then the bomb shell:" Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You proceed to write, "An order arrived [verbally of course]." Why do you say, "Of course"?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Being a bit cynical, probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I thought so, too. I thought so, too.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because quite a lot of significant orders in these days coming down from the UN came verbally to me and not in writing. Writing was always later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And then after the cynical comment, you continued to proceed to say, "to assist Serbs."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And it's the same words you used earlier today on page 25 that we just discussed. And here you also, in 1996, meant to cooperate and to support; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Then you proceed to say, "who had permission to proceed with the deportation of the population with their own vehicles." Correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Who had permission to proceed with that evacuation, or deportation, as you put it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it refers to the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, who did they get the permission from?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know. I know only -- later on, received written guidelines from the UN, and out of that document, I probably concluded that there was an arrangement between the UN and the Bosnian Serb army. And that's what I mean by they "had permission to." You could translate it that "it was agreed upon that they," et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, am I correct that, in fact, the verbal orders that you received were, in fact, to cooperate and support the departure. Those were your orders, were they not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the extent of my orders, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means that I don't recollect the exact verbs that I heard then which were in my orders, but that was the meaning of the orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If we can just turn to the last page of this --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: -- chapter or article that you wrote for the book, and it's the second full paragraph on that fourth page where you were asked the question, or you asked the question yourself, and you answered by saying, "Cooperate, support the departure; those were the orders."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Does that refresh your recollection that, indeed, those were specifically your orders?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I only tried to make clear that I did not recollect the exact words of my orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Now I'd like to turn to another topic, if I may, and that is the list of Muslim men that were put together, the 239, I believe it is, that --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually 251, but I did some bad counting then, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. 251. Who created that list, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The committee, so the representatives and the committee that we formed, made that list. They went around and registered the men.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Who requested that that list be made, initially?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Who was Jan van Hecke? Do you remember the name? Or Jan van Hecke.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Doesn't ring a bell to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to us what the purpose of the list was?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because we were looking for a way to give the man a form of more protection. I came to the old -- as I told before, Amnesty International did that before, and it was the only thing I could figure out that we could give them some more protection by making them known, giving them an identity.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Would it be correct that you explained the reason you were seeking to obtain those lists of men to the actual population at Potocari?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained it to the committee.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. And you would expect the committee to explain it to the rest of the population --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: -- naturally?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, there was an issue of approximately 60 or so Muslim men who refused to place their names on this list. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. That was reported to me by the committee.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Did the committee share with you what reasons they gave for not placing their names on the list?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What, if anything, did you do in response to obtaining that information?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the information that those 60 men did not want to be registered? Nothing. It's their own wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Wait a minute. Mr. Ostojic, you were not here when the witness was being asked the same questions by other counsel during these past two days; I understand that. That does not provide a justification for us to allow repetitive questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I agree, and I believe that they weren't repetitive; perhaps just for background. But I will move along, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's already explained that he can give us no information on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. May I proceed, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is it reasonable to assume that these 60 men did not want their name placed on the list because they didn't want the VRS or anyone to know that they were actually within the enclave?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't answer that question, sir. We don't need assumptions. We need clear, straightforward information from you, informed details and not assumptions.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I understand that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Make your submission later on, but you don't ask the witness to answer such a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, going back to the reporting, were your subordinates also required to report to you when they met with specific VRS military officers?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that goes within their obligation to report contact with the parties in any way, so yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know how many times Colonel Boering was kidnapped or held hostage during the January through July 1995 period?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stated before that the kidnapping situation is unknown to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So other than the one, possibly, in July, none other that you're aware of; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I'm aware of, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Specifically with meetings with VRS officers, is that something that you, yourself, as the second in command and in charge of operations, you'd be interested to know who your subordinates met with at any given time; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, and they did report when they came back, I told you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: On how many occasions did Colonel Boering report to you that he met with Mr. Beara?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Doesn't ring a bell to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you, sir, ever meet with Mr. Beara?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably not. I do not recollect a meeting with him, anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In fact, in none of your statements from 1995 to the present have I been able to find that you've ever mentioned that you met with Mr. Beara; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes. As I said, the name doesn't ring a bell to me. But I'm bad at names, but -- no. That is a no.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The meetings that were held at the Hotel Fontana prior to July of 1995 with various VRS military personnel, were they regularly scheduled meetings?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not regularly.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Were they meetings that you, from time to time, attended?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And why not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because it was -- I already, in fact, explained that. We had a system that the S5, then Major Boering, did that. Only when there were problems that he couldn't solve, I came in; and if I couldn't solve it, the colonel came in.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And isn't it true, sir, it was within his obligations and duties to report to you with whom he met, when he met, and what was discussed during the meeting with military officers or officials at Hotel Fontana, or anywhere, for that matter; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he reported that, whether to the colonel or to me, but then I got briefed by the colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's all I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Now, there is re-examination, I take it? Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: It's still morning. Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall being asked yesterday a question about an agreement on paper between Generals Mladic and Smith?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And that's at page 33 of yesterday's transcript, beginning at line 6. I believe you stated that you discovered that that had been reduced to writing after you returned to Holland.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Have you ever seen that actual document, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I even had a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And who -- can you describe for the Trial Chamber the circumstances under which you were furnished a copy of that document.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it came out of our gear when we were back in Holland, in a way, but I don't know the source. I don't know how I got the copy, but I found it within my extended paperwork I still had; not very organised but it was in between it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'd like to show you --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we can have displayed on e-court - I believe it's in there now; if not, I can just put it on the ELMO - it's P02265, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you have an image on your screen, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I would just ask you to take a moment to read this first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Perhaps we can - exactly, thank you - scroll down slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If you would just say when you're ready to ...

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. If we could see the second page, please.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, looking at the signature lines, do you see the dates underneath?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the 19th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Signed by both generals; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, while we have this page here, why don't we just talk about it and then we can go back to the first page. We will just take it out of order for a second, as long as we have it on the screen. The bullet or item at the top refers to what, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The movement of DutchBat out of -- as far as I can see, the movement of DutchBat out of the enclave into the area of Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And going back to the first page, if we could, do you know what the first item refers to, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was access to the SLC and the reception points, probably manned the locations where Muslim forces or men were held by the BSA. At least that's what I understood of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And the second point?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That refers -- based on the date, it refers to the POWs being in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And the date that's referred to there is?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 15th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And the third item?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, making it possible that UNHCR take up his supply task for the population in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: This is pure assumption, in our submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you assuming, Mr. Franken, or are you being positive in your answers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my answers I used wrongly the word "assume," but I refer to, as far as I know, the facts, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. You may proceed, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the next couple of items, item 4 and 5, having read those items, do those items apply to the situation that you were facing following the fall of the Srebrenica enclave, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it does not.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how about item 6, sir? Can you describe your understanding of that item, please.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as Srebrenica was concerned, in that phase, that was not applicable any more or not needed any more, and I mean UNHCR coming in with the humanitarian help.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And why was it not applicable any more?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the population was already gone then.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So, referring to item 7, what is that about, to your knowledge and understanding, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That concerns DutchBat, as far as it's still within the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And 7(A)?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That refers to the wounded still in custody of Medecins Sans Frontieres in our compound, as it refers to the wounded in the hospital in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And item (B)?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Already done, because the women and children and elderly, lots of them who were still there, were in our compound and were a patient or -- yes, were a patient with MSF.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So does this document, to your knowledge, include any guidelines regarding transportation or assisting the process?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And that would be the process of evacuation or perhaps transportation.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I want to ask you a couple of questions, sir, about the UNHCR and their policy. On at least one occasion you were asked by my learned colleague about them turning away a convoy that had arrived. Do you recall those questions?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall the questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, when you learned that the UNHCR turned back one of their convoys, did you, at some point, also learn what their reasoning was, why they objected or what problem they had such that they turned the convoy back?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember one occasion where they turned the convoy back when they had to give to -- a Bosnian Serb check-point, they wanted diesel and the UNHCR did not want them to take diesel and then they returned. That was reported to me by the UNHCR representative within the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: What other reasons did you learn that they may have turned back a convoy?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the only reason I recollect, the only incident I recollect as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did you, in fact, have some difference of opinion with UNHCR about their decision to turn back a convoy?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I could not understand that. I probably, almost literally, said that, I remember, to that representative, that about 100 litres of diesel is of more importance than a starving 25.000 people. I could not understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I want to ask you some questions regarding the attempt at trade between the Muslim population and the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You were asked a number of questions about that. Do you recall what the nature of these items that were under discussion for trade were?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Anything but military supplies, anything but weapons or ammunition or so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And that would include basic necessities.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Food.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: As well as amenities.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, what, in your view, in your experience there, would have been the simplest way to supply the civilian population with those basic necessities?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be general, stop the convoy terror.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Finally, sir, you were asked, I believe, by my learned colleague Madam Fauveau about Ibrahim Nuhanovic. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I believe you testified - I'm sorry, I don't have the cite in front of me - that you saw him boarding one of the last convoys; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall whether Mr. Nuhanovic had any military-age sons?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He had a son who used to be a BiH soldier, as was told to me by the other son, the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We didn't --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is out of the framework of the counter, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. The objection is overturned, Madam Fauveau, because the witness was asked on cross-examination by one of you on this specific of Mr. Nuhanovic and his family being -- boarding one of the buses. So you may proceed with your questions, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, you've been asked questions on numerous occasions about your interactions with Mr. Nuhanovic and his son, about decisions you had to make concerning that family. Do you recall the statement you gave or the information you gave to the NIOD investigation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not all of it now, but I know I made statements there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, can you describe for the Court the discussions you had and the decisions that you had to make regarding that family?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, well, two moments that have to be described. One is that his elderly brother, the interpreter, repeatedly came to me and wanted his younger brother on a list that he could get out with the UN; and secondly was the meeting I had with his father who asked me to stop the evacuation. As I remember that, that was on the evening of the 12th. Yes. We tried, for individuals, to supply them with -- and that is an answer for the younger brother, individuals to make some UN ID so that we could let them see that they were part of the personnel. The problem with that was we didn't have the means to make things like that; and secondly, the information of who belonged to the local staff had already been presented to the Bosnian Serbs, so I had to make an alteration on that list. Secondly, the request of Mr. -- the elderly Mr. Nuhanovic to stop the evacuation, I explained to him why I couldn't. So I described to him -- probably he knew already himself. I described to him the problems we had with the refugees, humanitarian way, hygienic supplies, medical support, et cetera. So in the end, I explained to him that I had to choose for those 25.000, up to 30.000, women and children, knowing that I was jeopardising about 800 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, was Ibrahim Nuhanovic's wife also in the compound, to your knowledge, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: She was in the compound but not present at these meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: What did you tell Ibrahim Nuhanovic or Hasan Nuhanovic about your ability to bring the younger son out with DutchBat forces?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only one who came with that question was his brother, and I explained the same story, in fact, as I gave to you in my last answer. And I said that I didn't want to take the risk or jeopardise by not having a good identification of him, a UN identification, take the risk that the other civilians who had to go with us out of the enclave were -- the risk that they were taken out of the column as well. So I didn't want to jeopardise the other, what was it, 29 people in favour of that single boy.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what was the decision that the family made?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It proved that the family decided that they went together along on the buses. The exception was the interpreter, the elderly son. He stayed in the compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you remember how Mr. Nuhanovic, the elder, the father, said good-bye to you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was the first time that I was kissed by a man at the gate. He said farewell. He kissed me.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And have you received any information about the fate of the Nuhanovic family, sir, whether they are still alive or not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The only thing is that they are still missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any of the Defence teams that would like to put some questions to Mr. Franken on the document that was made use of? Yes, Ms. Condon.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I just seek leave to ask a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Proceed, then.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Mr. Franken, just in relation to the points at 7(A) and (B) of the agreement that you have in front of you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that, insofar as 7(B) was concerned, that had already occurred at the time that this document was signed.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Because, as we can see, it's signed the 19th of July by both parties. So, on its face, that particular requirement as to 7(A) seems to be superfluous; you'd agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Be that as it may, in your mind, when the evacuation was going on, that was pursuant to an agreement, as you understood it, between UNPROFOR and the VRS.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: In fact, in your mind, as I think you indicated to me yesterday, there were two steps. There was an agreement, and what you said was "the fact that it was laid down on paper, I discovered when I was back in Holland." On that very moment, being at the time the evacuation was occurring pursuant to UNPROFOR and the VRS, you didn't see the piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And so when you first saw this agreement --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: -- back in Holland, I presume -- I'll withdraw that. When you first saw this agreement, no doubt in your mind, that was confirming.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, confirming the thoughts I had about it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: The prior agreement.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Despite the fact that it's dated at a time when it had already happened.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: You'd agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon, you have further questions, too?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, just a quick question for the witness concerning the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, can you just look at paragraph 2 of this document.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot. I can't see paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: It's on the --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: The P number, Your Honour, is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is. It is there. It's paragraph 2 that wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Just paragraph 2 of the first page, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of the first page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. With respect to paragraph 2, I would like to know if the copy of that document that you found in your material once you were back home, whether it had this word slashed out, "today" replaced by "on"? Do you recall this, by any chance?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall that, sorry, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, this document, you said, was signed according to what you saw on page 2, on 19 July.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If you read this paragraph 2, which says that, "to provide DutchBat soldiers," and I'll read it completely, "to provide that the DutchBat soldiers leave Bratunac with their personal belongings and small arms." Whether we use "today 15 July 1995" or we use "on 15 July 1995," would you agree with me that this shows that this document, although it was signed on the 19th, those agreements were made long time before?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is logical to conclude that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, Mr. Bourgon. Any further interventions from the Defence teams? Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It follows, Mr. Franken, from what you've said, you have no idea where this agreement was signed?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So that's it. There are no questions from the Bench, which means, Mr. Franken, that your testimony ends here. On behalf of the Trial Chamber, and also of the Tribunal, I wish to thank you for having come over to testify in this trial, and I'm sure everyone will join me in wishing you a safe journey back to where you wish to go. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Now, Prosecution, Mr. Thayer, you have -- you can proceed which exhibits or documents do you wish to tender.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, the first document is P00453.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And this is a declaration signed at Hotel Fontana, dated 17 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Actually, Your Honour, that description is, I think, slightly incorrect. It's a declaration which was signed at the Potocari base, but refers to events at the Hotel Fontana.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We'll just make that correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I take it there are no objections from the Defence. I see none. Next?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Is P01897, that is the colour photograph showing the burning pile of belongings in the vicinity of the "White House".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No objections? Next?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Is P02057. That is the handwritten list of 239 or 51 names of Bosnian men within the DutchBat compound.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No objection? Next?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That is P02263, an order from then Major Franken to Captain Groen, dated 9 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No objections? Next?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: P02264, an order from Major Franken to Captain Groen dated 10 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No objection? Yes, next?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: PIC17, that is the overhead view of Potocari, marked by Mr. Franken during his testimony on 16 October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No objection? I need a clarification on this by Madam Registrar. Will this be one document, one exhibit, or will it be several? Because he put marks on the document on several occasions, and the last on the last occasion, I remember you standing up and telling me that will have a different number. So we need a clarification on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I've been informed that it's IC18, if that helps.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, the Prosecutor asked twice to sign the document -- I mean to make marks on the document. But all marks will be IC17. And then the Defence will make marks as well and will be IC18. So we will have two exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour when it's my turn I was going to ask that IC18 be admitted as well. It can be done now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's come to that one at a time. All right. This last document that you made use of during your re-examination, are you tendering it or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: At this time, Your Honour, I would tender it as P02265, that is, the agreement between Generals Smith and Mladic dated 19 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I take it there are no objections either on the admission of this document. So these seven documents that have been mentioned and tendered by the Prosecution are being so admitted with the respective number, P number, that has been indicated. Defence for Mr. Popovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We seek to tender ID35 and ID36.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. To be precise, make sure that we are talking of the same documents. First is a code cable from Akashi to Kofi Annan on the situation in Srebrenica; second, UNMO headquarters and the situation in BH.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objection from the Prosecution or any other of the Defence teams?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Not from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see no objection, so these three documents are admitted. Borovcanin Defence? Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. We have the text "In the Name of the Peace - A Retrospective," 4D41, for identification, and the order by General Rasim Delic dated 6 August 1995, and the ID number is 4D26. These are the documents that we would like admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Stojanovic. Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: None, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Objections from the other Defence teams? They are so admitted. Miletic Defence? Miletic. Madam Fauveau? I'm going through them according to the order they have been presented to me. So my apologies if Mr. Nikolic wanted to go first. Yes, Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I seek to tender Exhibit 5D76. It is a report, an UNMO report, dated 12th of July 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you. Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. None. It is so admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Fauveau, I remember you asked some questions with respect to passages appearing in NIOD report, or some statements without reading them to the witness, thereby those passages not appearing in the transcript and you are not tendering those documents. How are you going to deal with that case?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The documents were admitted during the testimony of Mr. Boering. This is the reason why I did not seek to tender them, because they are already in the case file.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's very helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. We take your word for it, Madam Fauveau. And we will proceed. Milan Gvero Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: IC18.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And that would be IC18, the map on which the witness Franken put further markings.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's the same as IC17 with the addition of the one body.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. No further documents? Mr. Haynes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Out of curiosity, I showed Mr. Franken a very short passage of the video of General Mladic and the APC which came from the Srebrenica trial video which I think has now been shown in its entirety in the course of these proceedings but has not been admitted into evidence. That's the position, according to the Prosecution case manager and the court officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. You probably are right. From my recollection, in fact, I think you are right. Do you wish to tender the part of the video, the footage that you made use of?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm happy if we simply redress the position with the video in its entirety. I don't want to put in a little passage just for the purpose of a little piece of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's the more sensible way of approaching it, but I have to ask you. Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Srebrenica trial video has actually been admitted - it's P2047 - in its entirety, as I understand it. So it is, in fact, in evidence. I think on some occasions counsel for the accused have admitted clips as separate exhibits on their own.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Also, for the record, I had no objections to the IC018, I think, or the number of the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. So that concludes this part of the proceedings. We will have the break now, and -- there are no other Defence teams that wish to tender other documents, are there? Okay. It seems not. So we'll have a 25-minute break, starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, sir. Welcome to this Tribunal. We have just over three-quarters of an hour left for today during which we will start with your testimony. But before you start giving evidence, our rules require that you enter a solemn declaration, equivalent to an oath in some jurisdictions, to the effect that, in the course of your testimony, you'll be speaking the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. Madam Usher is handing to you the text of the solemn declaration. Please read it out loud, and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. Please make yourself comfortable. Ms. Soljan, for the Office of the Prosecutor, will be examining you. She will then be followed by the various Defence teams. Expect to be here tomorrow and the day after, at least. Thank you. Ms. Soljan.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Lieutenant Colonel. Before we begin speaking, I'll remind you that, since we are speaking the same language today, we both need to keep in mind to speak slower, and you should pause before -- once my question is asked, you should pause a little bit, try to speak slowly, and I'll try to do the same on my end, after you're done. Lieutenant Colonel, could you please tell us your full name.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: I'm Vincentius Bernardus Egbers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you spell your last for the record, please.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: E-g-b-e-r-s.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you are currently serving in the Royal Marechaussee; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: What is your rank?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: I'm a lieutenant colonel.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And from 1988 to 1998, you were serving in the Royal Dutch Army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us, during that time, when you deployed to the Srebrenica enclave with DutchBat III.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please pause between question and answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: I went to the enclave at January 1995 and I left the enclave at July 24th, 1995, and I've been there between those two dates.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Thank you. What was your rank during your time of service at Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: I was a lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And what were your duties and responsibilities within the enclave as lieutenant?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: I was a platoon commander of the 3rd Platoon of the Charlie Company who was inside of the Potocari area.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And as platoon commander, what was your daily routine like?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: I had 30 soldiers who had to manage up to -- to be at an observation post, Observation Post Alpha. We have to patrol the area. And then, of course, I had some work at the headquarters of DutchBat.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Madam Usher, if I could ask to you display on e-court the exhibit with 65 ter number 1901, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the second microphone for the witness be turned on, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: From what I understand it's a rather large document and takes a while to download. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Can you see this document, Lieutenant Colonel?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Could you please describe for the Court what this area is, and in particular the pie-shaped yellow area.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: The north of the enclave, between Observation Post Romeo and Alpha, was the area that Charlie Company had to manage the OPs and patrolling. So the north is the Charlie Company. And we had three platoons. My platoon was the 3rd Platoon, and my area of responsibility was Observation Post Alpha and the area between Jaglici and Observation Post Mike. That's where my platoon was patrolling.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Could you indicate for the Court where exactly, or what letters represented the OPs you were in charge of on that map?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: OP Alpha. OP Mike was at that time, in the beginning, a non-permanent observation post. That's an observation post we would go to, deploy, and then after some time go back again.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And OP Mike, is that the observation post displayed in this document as with letter M?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: It is. It is in the north of the village Jaglici.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. What other observation posts were then under your command?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: None.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, you had said that your platoon was normally 30 people; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Now, was your platoon of that size around July 1995?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Unfortunately, it wasn't, because all the personnel travelling towards Zagreb, to be on a short break, was able to get out of the enclave, but unfortunately it wasn't -- did not have the permission to go back to the enclave again. So in July, one-third of my platoon was waiting in Zagreb for the permission to go back to the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And who was granting this permission; do you know?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: As far as I know, all clearance for transportation between Zagreb -- between Zvornik and Bratunac has to be by the authorities of the BSA.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Thank you. So in July of 1995, you had approximately 20 men under your command.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: In addition, were you also part of another unit within DutchBat at that time?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: During the fall, there was a short platoon, let's call it a reserve, a battalion reserve, that was in Potocari, ready to support the south of the enclave as OP Echo or OP Foxtrot were under attack. We were the ones with four APCs who were able to help in the south.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And, sir, this reserve battalion or reserve unit, was this a unit that existed normally? Was it in place already in January when you had arrived?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: This was a reserve -- these were APCs that were not in use at the time, so we took them together. There was a driver on it, a gunner, and a commander on each vehicle. So we had a few lieutenants left and other soldiers left to manage to get on the APCs, the armoured personnel carriers, and then be ready for any support in the south. But it wasn't fully with -- in an APC that can be, let's say, ten men. There were only three. And it was a temporary thing decided by the headquarters for anything to happen in the south.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in July of 1995, were you, in fact, a part of this reserve unit with these four APCs, or rather, were you using these four APCs in your capacity of a reserve unit, Lieutenant?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: At that time, the four APCs were under my command, and we went to the south to see whether we could help Observation Post Sierra and Uniform, who were in the south, nearby Observation Post Echo and Foxtrot. We went there and we made plans, what we could do to help them, in case of any attack.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Okay. Now let's turn briefly to the situation that arose when OP Echo fell. Can you please describe what happened to you specifically with respect to your responsibilities or duties after OP Echo fell in July.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: I remember the date, the time, very well because one of our soldiers was killed, and he was brought to Potocari with an APC. And then we got the order that night to go down to UN Bravo Company so that we could help this Captain Groen, who was in charge of the south of the enclave, with the Observation Post Sierra, Uniform, Echo and Mike. So I went down by the road from Potocari to Srebrenica and then I got the order, with two APCs, to ride down all the way up to Uniform so I could tell them where the Bosnian Serb army and the Muslim fighters were, whether inside the enclave or not. That's what I had to do at that time. So I drove down. And there were a few Bosnian Muslims who were stopping my APC at the time. They even threw a hand grenade at my APC. And then I went back to the Bravo Company, to Captain Groen, and Captain Groen then ordered me to go to another position. Later on, we call it Bravo 1; it's a blocking position. And it was on the way from Srebrenica to Cancari, to OP Alpha.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, I'll stop you for just a second.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Madam Usher, if I could please get displayed on the e-court the exhibit or document with 65 ter number 1902, please. If we could zoom in a little bit. It's not clear. Thank you. Now it's very good. Perhaps if you could just -- yes, that's perfect. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Now, sir - perhaps if Madam Usher could show our witness how to use the stylus - I'd like for you to indicate for us, please, with the use of the stylus, where this position of Bravo 1 was, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I apologise. I don't want to interrupt, but I believe it would be very helpful to know what date it was, because we don't have an exact date. Perhaps Ms. Soljan could ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Fair enough. I think -- yes, Ms. Soljan, you can do that either now or later.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Certainly. What the date arrival of ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's how I understood Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Okay. Sure. I will get that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think if we can zoom in further on this map, it will be more helpful.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: I think you can indicate for us first, perhaps, where Srebrenica is for us.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: That's why you've got to zoom in.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, can you indicate or tell the Court please what this area that you have just circled is.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: This is the road going from Srebrenica to OP Alpha, which was in a --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: I think you will actually have to point with the stylus in order to show the road.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: This is the road.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: And the road makes two turns by 180 degrees, first to the right and then to the left. And in the second angle to the left, that was Bravo 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Bravo 1 was in the second angle to the left. Could you indicate it with a little cross, please.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, against that little cross, he could write the words "Bravo 1," then, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. That should be enough.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Okay. Could you please tell us, for the record, what date did you first arrive at Bravo 1?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: That was July 8th.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Thank you. How long did you stay at Bravo 1?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: I stayed there for totally four days, but I had to go and -- go to the marketplace in Srebrenica a few days later.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know when that was, approximately, or precisely?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: That was on the 11th of July.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: On the 11th of July. And during the four days that you were at Bravo 1, can you tell us what you observed? What was happening?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Well, Bravo 1 was on top of a hill, so I could, very good, have a look at the south of the enclave. And I could see tanks, T-54 or 55, entering the enclave, fire a shot, and then go out of the enclave again.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Now, do you know whose forces these T-54/55 tanks belonged to?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: They belonged to the BSA, to the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And how did you know that, sir?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: I know that because there was a weapon collection point at the Bravo Company. There was just a few weapons of the -- ones that belonged to the Muslims were there. I saw, from outside the enclave, a tank enter the enclave, fire shots, and then go outside the enclave again, so that must be the BSA.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
