utterances.text: And in which direction was -- from which direction was this tank coming?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: It was coming from the east; entering the enclave, firing at Srebrenica, my position, and then going out of the enclave again.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Could you please indicate with the stylus precisely what direction -- with an arrow, what direction the tank would be coming in.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Okay. Maybe you could write the words "tank" just so we know that's ...

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: So this is what I saw: I saw a tank entering the enclave, firing shots. And we've learned that a tank, T-54/55, is only to shoot about 1.500 metres, but when it's -- when the barrel is up in the air, it can be used as a piece of artillery as well. So that's what they did. They fired directly but also used it as a piece of artillery. What I also saw in the south was a village, Pusmulici, and I could see from my position houses burning, people entering the houses even with dogs, and that's in this side of the -- on the line at --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: If you could please circle that.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: That's Pusmulici?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Pusmulici.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Now, do you recall when, exactly, you saw people?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: That was the second day. That was the 9th of July.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And did you know who these people entering the houses in Pusmulici were?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: They were BSA, coming out of the enclave and going to the villages, and then burning them or trying to get into them with dogs. We saw that because we had binoculars with us at Bravo 1. And we reported everything we saw to Captain Groen, who was in charge of the south of the enclave at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Were these individuals wearing uniforms?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: As I could see at that time, they were using -- wearing camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And did they have weapons with them?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: They had also weapons with them, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. Sir, if you could please sign this document at the bottom so that we can save it.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. From this position at Bravo 1, what was the purpose of this position -- was there a purpose to this position other than just observation?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Well, at first it was observation, and later on it became a line not to be crossed by the BSA. So we had an order. To be seen from the air very clearly, we had to be an imaginary line between the Bosnian Serbs and the Muslims in the north. So that's why we were there, with our white vehicles, standing on top of the hills.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Is this line equivalent to a blocking position, or is that something different?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: No. At that time, we had to make a statement. I believe at that time there was an air strike coming for everything that was on the south of our blocking positions. So we had to report everything that was going on in the south to Captain Groen. And then it's a signal to the Bosnian Serbs not to cross the line between the blocking positions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Okay. During the time that you were at Bravo 1, were you ever directly targeted by the forces coming from the south, you or any of your soldiers?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Yes. I was there, and ten minutes later there was a mortar fire or fire from a tank which was on our position. Then we had to go back to another position that was the first angle I told you on the map. That was the second position where we could still have a sight on the south, but we were not on top of the hill again. So we went there. But I got the order to go back again and then we got shelled again. So we were shelled.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Okay. Do you remember approximately when this shelling took place?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: It took place on the second day I was there, the 9th of July and the 10th of July.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And was anybody injured as a result of this shelling?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: There was. There was a -- one of my privates was injured but only slightly injured. But the APC was damaged by that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Okay. And this was an injury coming from mortar or shelling from the BSA forces; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you were also saying that the tanks were firing in the direction of Srebrenica. Did you see any hits? Did you know about any injuries of people in Srebrenica itself?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: I could see a tank firing at Srebrenica and I saw the place where the grenade hit the ground, but I couldn't see whether there were any people injured by the shelling.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Okay. And while you were at Bravo 1 or near that location, were you aware that close-air support was being summoned?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: That's what my commander told me. He told me, "You have to have a forward air controller in your position because your position is that good that it can have a clear view on the south of the enclave. And there will be a NATO strike from the F-16s," or even a gunship is mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And did you, indeed, receive close-air support?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. There were two F-16s who were forwarded to a target near the south of the Srebrenica area, and they tried to hit a T-54/55.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know what date this took place?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: This was -- I thought it was the 11th of July.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Okay. So it would have been the fourth day --

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: It was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: -- of your stay at Bravo 1. And what happened next? Once this close-air support arrived, what did you have to do or what did the reserve unit have to do?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: I then had the opportunity, because of the air strike, to go to the Observation Post Bravo -- excuse me, the headquarters of the Bravo Company, and at that place, there were a lot of people gathering around the UN base. There was every vehicle that could drive. There were hundreds of people waiting for the vehicles to drive them to safety. At that time I ordered all my men to walk with the refugees towards the north, and I took all the sick and wounded from the hospital of the -- the hospital of Srebrenica that was under Medecins Sans Frontieres on my APC, and I tried to drive with the people to the north, to Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Just to take you back a moment. You had said that the close-air support did hit something; correct? It hit a tank?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: There was a tank firing at me, and the tank, T-54/55, was between my position and Srebrenica, Bravo Corps. From my position, the tank was hit or it was demolished, so it couldn't fire at me any more. So that was the point when it was safe for me to go and to help the Bravo Company with the refugees.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Okay. And then you were placing people on the APC and you started moving towards Potocari; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Well, the first APC was on the front of all the people who were trying to go to safety at Potocari. We took them with us. And it was a very extraordinary situation of course. It was 35 degrees; it was very hot. There was even a mother who handed over her baby to me so I could take care of that baby, but of course I'm glad that I took the mother as well on my APC. There were mentally ill people on my APC. We were shelled at that time, on the left and the right side of the road, by mortar, so everybody wanted to leave Srebrenica and go to Potocari. There were people carrying each other on this 5.000-metre road to Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Sir, you just said you were shelled by mortar on the left and on the right. What direction was this mortar coming from?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: It was fired from the south and it was luckily not on the road but near the road. And it came from the south, from the BSA.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Okay. How would you characterise this firing? Was it continuous, would you say, or sporadic?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: It happened four or five times and then we drove to the north. So I don't know whether it happened after I left.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Could you tell the type of artillery or weapons used in the shelling? Was it purely mortar or was there anything else?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: There was just mortar fire from the BSA side.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And what resulted from the firing of that artillery, mortar, have on the people in the column of refugees from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: They were very, very scared, of course. They didn't know what to do and everybody asked us, "What should we do now?" And then we took -- we tried to get everybody in the direction of Potocari, but they didn't feel that it was safe being near the border of the enclave in the north. So we drove with them, we walked with them, to take them towards Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And did you eventually succeed in getting to Potocari with this column of refugees?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: I did. I delivered all the sick and wounded people from the hospital to our own small hospital at the headquarters of DutchBat, and then after four days, we stayed for a few hours at the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Do you recall what time of day it was when you arrived at Potocari?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: It was the fourth day, so it's July 11th.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And do you know what time of day it was?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. It was in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And what was the situation like in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Well, it was very, very hot. We had no water to give to the people. There were thousands of people gathering around the UN base. We tried to get as much of them inside the headquarters, and then even outside the headquarters there has to be a temporary UN base line where they could rest for a while. It was a very, very panic situation at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And what did you do that night?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Well, after four days, we tried to get some sleep at that time. We didn't sleep for four days, so we had a few hours of rest.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Okay. And so the next day, the 12th of July, after you woke up, what happened? What was the first thing you observed or the first task you were tasked with?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Well, at some times there were buses coming in, inside the enclave, and the buses, we didn't know what to expect, but those buses, they were coming and there was -- the deportation was on its way. There was the first buses for the first convoy for the first deportation. So I went there and I looked at things, what -- whether to help or not, on the outside of the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Okay. And did you, at some point, receive orders?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Well, yes, I did. Major Franken told me to get ready for the first convoy. He tried to get a soldier on every bus, but he only had permission to send a vehicle with two UN peacekeepers together with all the buses. So I took my water, my sleeping bag, my stuff, I put it inside a vehicle, and I just waited where the buses went to, and I rode with the buses to an unknown destination. We didn't know where to go to. My only orders were to follow the bus and to report what happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And who was in these buses?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: I was at the first convoy, with General Mladic standing there with a TV crew, and in these buses were women and children, and they were there, not knowing where to go to as well. In the first convoy, there was a UN car in front of the convoy, then there were buses, and then there was my own car at the end of the convoy.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Okay. Did any other Dutch officers accompany you in escorting this convoy?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Well, there were two officers in the front and I was with a colleague in the second car at the end of the convoy.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Now, I'd like you to describe your journey on that first convoy from Potocari. What did you see along the way?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Well, as you know, we first entered the village of Bratunac, when we left Srebrenica, and at that time there was a party going on in Bratunac and there were a lot of people celebrating, drinking and screaming and yelling and throwing at buses that were driving through Bratunac. So at that time, it was completely strange, of course, because we had a very giant crisis and then there was a -- we are entering a party. When we left Bratunac, we saw a lot of BSA soldiers gathering around the road. They stopped us, pointed their gun at us, and wanted some of our materials. For example, our helmet or our weapon or our bullet-proof vest. And it's strange, but I could -- because I was a lieutenant at the time, the BSA respected the ranking at that time. I say "You don't steal from a lieutenant," and I could drive on with the buses. But it didn't work all the time, so we -- they have stolen some equipment from us. And leaving Bratunac, I saw one of the buses had a breakdown, trouble of the engine, of course, and the other buses drove on with one of our cars and I decided to stay with the bus that broke down. All the women and children were in the bus, but I've asked the driver to open the doors and get everybody out, because it was it was very, very hot. And I gave all my medicine and all my water to the women and children on the bus. It was a strange situation. There was even a photographer coming to make photos from us. He wanted to have nice pictures with the women and children laughing. It was very strange. They even wanted to borrow my car to get a new bus.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: The women and children at that time that were standing outside of the bus. What state were they in?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Well, of course, like me, they were very uncertain of things that should happen. They were very, very scared of what might happen. They were not informed about anything. There was a bus breaking down. They saw me, because they were coming, other civilians, from the -- from the villages in the neighbourhood, coming to join us at the bus. So I just stood there, tried to separate them and say, "Okay, we've got to go on as soon as possible. We've got to leave this site."

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Now, Madam Usher, if I could get on e-court, please, or rather display on e-court, document 2111, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Now, sir, you were just telling us about the bus that had broken down shortly after you left Bratunac. Could you indicate or tell us, approximately, by looking at the map, whereabouts this bus broke down?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: I think it broke down in the area of Glogova. Can I point it out to you on the map?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think that will be better.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It must be around there, leaving Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Okay. And could you please indicate, then, by an arrow which way you continued with the bus.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Perhaps I'm jumping ahead of myself. But did the bus, indeed, get repaired?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: It didn't get repaired but it got replaced. So there came another bus and we drove all the way --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: -- to the west.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. If you could perhaps sign this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, as you continued along this road, was there anything in particular that you observed?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: I then saw a lot of infantry along the road, facing south, facing the woods. They were heavily armed. And I even saw some anti-aircraft machine-guns on a vehicle in the village here, about Sandici. So about every ten metres there were infantry soldiers facing the south; some were firing. And they were stopping us, letting the bus drive on, but actually stopping us and looking what was going on inside the car. So they stopped us, pointed the gun at us, and all along we had to drive on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Could you tell what forces these soldiers belonged to?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Along the road there were vehicles with a giant wolf head on the side of it, so that's the only thing I can say. There is a wolf head - I guess it was the Drina Wolves - on the vehicles, and the vehicles were standing near the road. And there was a lot of infantry dressed in infantry camouflage suits, facing south.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: These infantry soldiers, did they actually fire in the direction facing south?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: At that time they didn't fire as much, but I saw some firing.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And did you hear any return fire from the woods, from the position south?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: No. I've never heard any gun -- any sound of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: How many soldiers would you estimate you saw in the stretch between, say, Bratunac and Konjevic Polje?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: There were hundreds.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: How were they spaced? Could you describe that for us?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Well, they were making a line, so every 10 metres there were some soldiers, two or three, and then there was, let's say, 20 metres between the groups of soldiers. So, in my opinion, there must have been more than 100 at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And they were all dressed, as you said, in camouflage uniforms --

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: They were.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Now, where did the buses then continue on to?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Well, there was a roadblock near Konjevic Polje, so we had to turn south there, to the village of Milici, and the buses all drove south.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Okay. Now, on your way south, did you observe anything out of the ordinary?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: I saw some men with -- walking around or near the street with their hands in their neck and they were walking. And when I saw a football field on my right, I saw men, Muslim men, gathering on the football field. They were sitting on their knees with their hands in their neck. And there was even a table. And everything I saw I radioed all the way to OP Alpha, because nobody knew where the buses went to and nobody knew where we went to. So we always had radio contact with OP Alpha, Observation Post Alpha. And I -- everything that we had to deal with - the stopping and the men firing - was reported by me to OP, observation post, Alpha. And also, the football field full of men sitting on their knees with their hands in their neck, lined up.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Could you estimate what the number of these men sitting on their knees with their hands on their necks was?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: There were between 100 and 200.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Okay. Were they guarded?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: There were Bosnian Serbs in that neighbourhood at that time, and there were men on the football field standing near the men and they were in camouflage uniforms, so that must be the BSA. I saw the men walking on the road towards the football field, from the north to the south. And, of course, when I passed the football field, from the south to the north.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Okay. And these men who were in -- that is 150 to 200 men who were in the football field, what kind of outfits were they wearing? Could you --

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: To me, they were just civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: And their stuff, the things they brought with them, were gathered nearby the football field. So the bags they were carrying.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: I could show one more exhibit depending on if we do have enough time to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have about three minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: I think an exhibit can be shown in that amount of time. If you wouldn't mind please putting on e-court 65 ter document 1664, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Now, sir, can you describe for the Court what you see on this picture.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: On this picture I see a road going to Nova Kasaba and I see the football field nearby the road, and on that football field the men were held.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In future, please try to avoid using images like this or other documents for that matter which already have indications on them. Please try to avoid that. I think we had made that clear some time back.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: My apologies, Your Honour. We'll do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Now, Lieutenant Colonel, where did you go from this area? Where did the buses continue?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: The buses, they drove on, on the way towards Milici, and then turned right towards Kladanj.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And was this your final destination?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Well, that's where the buses stopped. When I got there with the bus, the other buses were waiting there. It was in the middle of a wood. So the women and children on the first convoy, a lot of the women were glad to see me there because they thought they were killed in the middle of the wood. They made this sign to me. I don't know how to describe that, but ...

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Just for the record, the sign is indicated by?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: A finger.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: The forefinger going from the left, from the direction of the left shoulder to the right shoulder, across the neck. What did you understand that sign to mean, sir?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Well, those women who signed that to me thought that they would be killed in that forest.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And what did happen, sir?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS BERNARDUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Well, I left my vehicle and I walked towards a point where they would let everybody out of the buses. And the two UN colleagues who were in the first convoy, the first bus, excuse me, the first vehicle, they left their vehicles and walked with them towards Bosnian Serb -- excuse me, the Muslim areas. So there, everybody got out and walked their way. And what I only did was checking whether everybody could get out of the bus and be able to walk at the way out of the Bosnian Serb areas.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we need to stop here for today. Lieutenant Colonel, we will meet again tomorrow morning. With that, I think I wish you all good afternoon and good evening. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 19th day of October, 2006, at 9.00 a.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
